entries.title: CBP officer tells jury he met sex workers but 'never raped anyone' — then brags he 'got a good workout in'
entries.summary: <p>U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officer<b> </b>Luis Uribe told a jury Tuesday he<b> </b>“never raped anybody.”</p><p>He visited prostitutes and hid it from his wife, he said. But he assured jurors that “no means no.” And<b> </b>“stop means stop.”<b> </b>And he swore he “never hit a woman”<b> </b>in his life — “ever.”</p><p>Then, when a prosecutor asked the federal officer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >accused of sexual assault</a> whether he’d used “physical fitness time”<b> </b>to get away from work for one of his alleged attacks, Uribe quipped in front of the jury, “I still got a good workout in.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/14/luis-uribe-cbp-sex-work-rape" >Customs officer was offered free sex to stop gunpoint rapes, sex worker testifies</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“You’re describing the rape … as a good workout?” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan<b> </b>Shih<b> </b>asked Uribe, incredulously.</p><p>“It wasn’t a rape,” Uribe shot back. “It was consensual sex.”</p><p>Uribe spent a little more than an hour trying to explain himself Tuesday, as his trial nears its end at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. Prosecutors and defense attorneys have each rested their case, setting the stage for closing arguments and jury deliberations.</p><p>But first, Uribe told jurors he’d been threatened<b> </b>by a supervisor in a Chinese prostitution ring who asked him repeatedly for help with immigration issues, only to have him shoot her down.</p><p>He said the the woman wound up warning him by text message, “if you don’t help me with all my immigration issues — help my boss — it’s going to be bad for you. I suggest you help me. If you don’t help me, I’m going to tell my sisters to testify against you.”</p><p>Now, prosecutors have accused Uribe of six attacks<b> </b>in Schaumburg and Naperville<b> </b>between February and October 2022, when Uribe was assigned to O’Hare Airport. He is charged with 10 counts of deprivation of civil rights under color of law<b> </b>and one count of brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence.</p><p>Defense attorney Michael Clancy told the jury last week <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" >there’s no evidence</a> Uribe robbed and raped four women, as prosecutors allege.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became ‘perfect mark’ for prostitution ring, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Uribe told jurors Tuesday his encounters with prostitutes were always consensual. He said that, if he knew he’d be patronizing a prostitute after work, he would leave all of his “tools”<b> </b>behind — including his handcuffs, baton,<b> </b>knife and gun.</p><p>“I never threatened to shoot anybody,” Uribe testified.</p><p>Sometimes he offered jurors details about his visits with prostitutes, including one encounter he said ended with a hug.<b> </b>But when pressed by Shih on whether he had sex with his alleged victims, Uribe told him,<b> </b>“I don’t recall the specific instances. I paid for sex. So my belief is, I did.”</p><p>Uribe also explained his relationship with the purported supervisor he said threatened him in 2022. He told jurors that, after his first sexual encounter with her, she learned he worked in immigration enforcement. He said her face lit up “like she hit the jackpot or something.”</p><p>Then he had more than 10 additional encounters with her in 2021 and 2022, he told the jury. Every time, he said,<b> </b>she asked for help with immigration issues for herself or others.</p><p>That <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/14/luis-uribe-cbp-sex-work-rape" target="_blank" >woman testified Monday</a>, and she acknowledged failing to tell the feds about many of her visits with Uribe. She also denied having any kind of supervisory role in the prostitution ring.</p><p>Uribe said he eventually met with that woman at a seafood buffet in Hoffman Estates. During the meeting, he said, she had him speak with her boss using a video app on her phone.</p><p>“The boss wanted to know how she could come into the U.S., because she was stuck in China, and how she could get more girls into the U.S., because they were also stuck in China,” Uribe explained.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" >In CBP officer’s rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: ‘He showed a badge’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Uribe insisted to the jury that, at the time of the meeting, there were no flights from China coming into the United States because of COVID-19. The meeting purportedly took place in March 2022, and Shih later challenged Uribe on the claim.</p><p>“I do recall them telling me, ‘How do I get into the U.S. from China, because there’s no flights,’” Uribe told the prosecutor.</p><p>It was months later, in October 2022, that the purported supervisor sent her threatening text message, according to Uribe.</p><p>During his cross-examination, Shih pointed out that all of Uribe’s alleged victims were Chinese. They didn’t speak fluent English. And they all had ties to illegal activity.</p><p>He told Uribe, “it would be less likely that anybody would believe them. … That’s why you preyed on them?”</p><p>“How did I prey on them?” Uribe retorted. “I didn’t prey on nobody.”</p>

entries.title: Thrilling Chicago, Pete Crow-Armstrong, Caleb Williams ‘want to give people something to look forward to’
entries.summary: <p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" >a wild season-opener</a>, <b>Caleb Williams</b> and the Bears have the Chicago area making Super Bowl plans.</p><p>The city’s hoping <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/15/connor-bedard-blackhawks-captain-best-player-face-of-franchise-leadership" >new Blackhawks captain</a> <b>Connor Bedard</b> will be handed the Stanley Cup one day.</p><p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> is on the verge of a 40-40 season, with his Cubs still eyeing a World Series win.</p><p>And that’s this week.</p><p>It might just be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/04/cubs-bears-bulls-chicago-sports-pete-crow-armstrong-caleb-williams-caleb-wilson-matas-buzelis" >that new era in Chicago sports</a>.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong started Tuesday just three stolen bases away from doing something that’s only been done six times previously in baseball history. He’s the MVP favorite in the regular season’s closing days, with his eyes squarely on what the Cubs can do once the lights get brighter in October.</p><p>You know, the same month when Williams will be slinging it on Sundays and Bedard’s Blackhawks will be in the opening days of their new campaign.</p><p>If you’re a sports fan, this is one of the best times of the year.</p><p>If you’re a Chicago sports fan these days, maybe even more so.</p><p>“We love this part of the year,” Crow-Armstrong said after Monday’s win over the Braves. “Not every city gets to look forward to all four major sports in such a small window like we get to here.</p><p>“We pay a lot of attention. I’m staying in here as long as possible pregame while Sunday football is going on.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is coming at Bears season a little differently than most of the city’s football fans.</p><p>He’s friends with Williams, and the quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/03/pete-crow-armstrong-nl-player-of-the-month-august-alex-bregman-stats-kevin-gausman-brewers" >showed up to a Cubs game last month</a> with Bulls stars <b>Matas Buzelis</b> and <b>Caleb Wilson</b>, supporting Crow-Armstrong and watching him homer from behind the Cubs’ dugout.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has shown up on the sidelines at Soldier Field, too, and the pair’s friendship — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/01/19/blackhawks-jets-caleb-williams-pete-crow-armstrong-connor-bedard-jonathan-toews" >they took in a Blackhawks game</a> earlier this year — only draws more attention to what the city’s two biggest sports stars and their contemporaries are capable of.</p><p>“It still kind of is trippy, but it’s cool that people appreciate us being friends,” Crow-Armstrong said. “We’ve definitely talked about what we want to build here together. But that all stems from a genuine appreciation of each other’s abilities and craft and how we make stuff happen.</p><p>“It’s agreed upon by all of us that we want to give people something to look forward to.”</p><h3><b>Miller out of time</b></h3><p>The Cubs are shutting down righty reliever <b>Shelby Miller</b>, who was working back from elbow surgery and was speculated as someone who could help the bullpen.</p><p>But Miller won’t be making an 11th-hour return to the majors this year, even after impressing the Cubs with his relatively speedy recovery; he was signed to a two-year deal without much expectation that he’d pitch this season.</p><p>Miller, a 13-year major league vet who posted a 2.74 ERA with the Diamondbacks and Brewers last season, had a 7.59 ERA in 13 minor league rehab appearances.</p><p>“At this point, the risk outweighs what reward there would be from keeping him going and pushing him to pitch in this environment,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Tuesday. “It’s just a risk that we agreed together not to take.</p><p>“We’ve got a healthy player, we’ve got a player ready for spring training going into next season, and we’re excited about that.</p><p>“He’s in a good spot. But he’s in a spot that you’re at after you’ve worked your butt off to get there. It’s time to stop and just give him a break.”</p><h3><b>Rained out</b></h3><p>A Tuesday rainout prevented shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> from beginning his minor league rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa. The Cubs were hoping Swanson would play in a couple games and return to the big league team Friday.</p>

entries.title: Redoing the rankings for the Class of 2022: Braden Huff is still No. 1
entries.summary: <p>Most men’s basketball players from Illinois in the high school Class of 2022 have used up their NCAA eligibility at this point.</p><p>Or have they? Several are still in the mix because they redshirted early in their college careers for developmental or injury reasons. And now some courts are weighing in on just who can or can’t play this upcoming season following the adoption of the NCAA’s “five-for-five” rule, which allows student-athletes to play five seasons of college sports.</p><p>In any case, it’s a fitting time to look back on what was considered a solid class through the lens of the last four years.</p><p>Here’s a re-ranking of the top players from the Class of 2022, minus former Thornton swingman Ty Rodgers, once the state’s No.  2-ranked prospect, who probably still would be in the top five if not for a series of devastating injuries that changed his career trajectory:</p><h3>1. Braden Huff, Gonzaga</h3><p></p><h3>(Glenbard West)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 1</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Injuries have slowed his overall impact, but averaging 17.8 points and 5.6 rebounds last season for a college powerhouse keeps him in the top spot. A big final season is expected from the 6-11 forward, who led Glenbard West to a state title as a senior.</p><h3>2. Nick Martinelli, Northwestern</h3><p></p><h3>(Glenbrook South)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 8</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Originally headed to Elon before a coaching change there, the always over-achieving forward quieted doubters after switching to NU and the Big Ten. Martinelli twice led the conference in scoring and finished his career with 1,787 points.</p><h3>3. Robbie Avila, Saint Louis </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Oak Forest)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 10</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Avila, a 6-10 center, became a bit of a sensation, scoring nearly 2,000 points between Indiana State and Saint Louis.</p><h3>4. Caden Pierce, Purdue </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Glenbard West)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 5</b></h3><h3></h3><p>His stellar college career has included an NCAA Tournament appearance, the Ivy League Player of the Year Award and more than 1,000 career points — and the 6-7 forward still has his final season left at Purdue.</p><h3>5. Tavari Johnson, Akron </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Lyons)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 11</b></h3><h3></h3><p>A point guard, Johnson dazzled the last two years in the MAC, leading the league in scoring last season with 19.7 points per game) while fueling a team that reached the NCAA Tournament. Will he be eligible for one more season at Charleston after transferring?</p><h3>6. Zach Cleveland, Normal </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Liberty)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 9</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Cleveland, a 6-7 forward, was an absolute stat-sheet stuffer in college (1,220 points, 749 rebounds and 569 assists) and won Conference USA Player of the Year as a senior.</p><h3>7. NJ Benson, DePaul </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Mount Vernon)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 12</b></h3><p>He’s penciled in for an extra year at Georgetown after a productive four NCAA seasons — two at Missouri State and the last two at DePaul. The 6-8 big man averaged 11.7 points and 7.6 rebounds for the Blue Demons.</p><h3>8. Jalen Quinn, Drake </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Tuscola)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 7</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After playing a small role at Loyola for three years, the 6-3 guard exploded as a senior at Drake, leading the Missouri Valley Conference in scoring with 19.7 points per game last season.</p><h3>9. Bobby Durkin, Minnesota</h3><h3></h3><h3>(Glenbard West)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 14</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After a year of prep school following high school and solid production at Davidson for two seasons, Durkin, a 6-7 forward, averaged 10.2 points at Minnesota as a junior.</p><h3>10. Cooper Noard, Cornell</h3><h3></h3><h3>(Glenbrook South)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 18</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Noard, a guard, had a somewhat overlooked career in the Ivy League, which he led in scoring with 18.7 points per game last season.</p><h3>11. Jaden Schutt, Kansas State</h3><h3></h3><h3>(Yorkville Christian)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 3</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Schutt will finish his career at Kansas State after two years at Duke and two at Virginia Tech. The 6-5 guard averaged 7.7 points in each of the last two seasons in the ACC.</p><h3>12. Xavier Amos, Loyola </h3><h3></h3><h3>(Young)</h3><h3></h3><h3><b>Rank in 2022: 4</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It has been a topsy-turvy college career for the 6-8 forward because of injuries. He took off as a sophomore at NIU, transferred to Wisconsin, where he barely saw the floor, then played last season with the Ramblers, averaging 11.1 points but in only 19 games.</p>

entries.title: Cubs want a whole lot more than last year’s quick playoff exit: ‘It’s time to do it again and do it better’
entries.summary: <p>The wild-card standings are tight enough that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> don’t yet know where they’ll be when the playoffs start in a couple weeks.</p><p>They know where they’d like to be. They’d like to be playing hosts at Wrigley Field.</p><p>But that’s not enough for this group, not after they got to experience a playoff series — and a playoff series win — at the Friendly Confines last fall.</p><p>After moving past the Padres in the wild-card round, they were dispatched by the division-rival Brewers in the NLDS, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >something that left a bad taste in their mouths</a> and has served as fuel for their fire.</p><p>Fans’ expectations are always high, and a similar result a year later won’t be enough for them.</p><p>It definitely won’t be enough for the Cubs’ clubhouse.</p><p>“That’s what we all prepare for,” center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong said Monday of bringing playoff baseball back to the North Side. “We talked about it last year, I talked about wanting to do that, and we did it.</p><p>“If last year is a result, then it’s got to be better. Now that we gave people a taste of playoff baseball again, it’s time to do it again and do it better.”</p><p>The Cubs won’t be bettering their second-place finish in the NL Central, with the Brewers starting Tuesday 9½ games up with only a handful of games to play. And their jockeying with the Phillies — not to mention the Padres and Diamondbacks hot on their heels — might mean a road trip for the postseason’s first round.</p><p>Of course, the Cubs won’t alter their championship-level aspirations because of the city they’re playing in as October begins.</p><p>“Does everybody want to play at home as many games as we can? Absolutely,” manager Craig Counsell said at the close of last month. “Are we going to shy away from a challenge on the road? Nope.</p><p>“That’s how we look at it, and that’s how every competitor looks at it.”</p><p>Counsell’s tenure as skipper comes with high expectations, given the big money the Cubs spent to lure him from the Brewers. He hasn’t been able to clear the hurdle of his former employers yet.</p><p>But new arrivals have seen Counsell as a tone-setter, of sorts, for this group, one that’s been focused and committed to approaching each day anew all summer.</p><p>“It starts with him and the preparedness that he has, the selflessness that he has, and making sure every guy on the team is put in the right position to succeed,” lefty pitcher David Peterson said. “I think that trickles down. It trickles down to the coaching staff. It trickles down to us.</p><p>“It’s something you can see from the other side. I saw it when I was with the Mets. It’s just a group that plays for each other. They stick together.</p><p>“We have 26 … guys that are pulling the rope in the same direction and are committed to winning as many ballgames as we can.”</p><p>The Cubs woke up Tuesday with the best offense and the best defense in baseball, showing they’re capable of doing what they’ve had their eyes on since the spring.</p><p>Whether they actually do it or not comes next.</p><p>Playing the NL East-leading Braves this week is beneficial, said lefty starter Matthew Boyd, with the Cubs getting a taste of the kind of competition they’ll face in the playoffs.</p><p>To win a playoff series, when the lights get their brightest, the Cubs will need to iron out their pitching issues. They might be as good as it gets with the bats and the gloves, but their pitching has been inconsistent. An at-times impressive group of starters has swung between looking like a playoff force and a playoff liability, while the bullpen is struggling to stabilize amid a late-season stumble.</p><p>But the team’s confidence? Not an issue.</p><p>“We feel good,” Boyd said. “This time of year, there’s always a lot of emphasis put on it, obviously, rightfully so. It’s right before the playoffs. But we feel good.</p><p>“There’s enough that we’re getting close to start clicking on, and it’s exciting. I still believe our best baseball is ahead of us, and we feel like we’re stepping into it.”</p>

entries.title: New-and-improved David Sandlin should have staying power in White Sox' rotation
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> haven’t had a pitcher work six innings in their last 23 games. So when it comes to assessing whether right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b> will get another chance to start after not allowing an earned run in 5⅔ innings Sunday, manager <b>Will Venable</b> didn’t waste time answering.</p><p>‘‘We just take this series by series,’’ Venable said. ‘‘But I would say he has earned another opportunity, for sure. I think that’s safe to say.’’</p><p>Beyond the Sox’ immediate need for results in the last 11 regular-season games, Sandlin clearly returned from his latest time at Triple-A Charlotte as a different pitcher. Despite his high-90s velocity and offseason work on a <b>Davis Martin</b>-style kick changeup, Sandlin couldn’t pump four-seamers to major-league hitters without getting hurt and lacked the tools to retire left-handers in his previous stints with the Sox.</p><p>‘‘Sat down with [senior adviser to pitching <b>Brian</b>] <b>Bannister</b> in Triple-A . . . right after the All-Star break,’’ Sandlin told the Sun-Times. ‘‘Just talking about introducing [my sweeper] to lefties early in counts, backdooring it. We really hammered that home. It showed success and makes the hitter need to lean out over the plate, and then I can take a shot inside.’’</p><p>Combined with tweaking the shape of his cutter to make it harder and shorter to mirror his fastball better, Sandlin has evolved his game in a way many hard-throwers have to accept at the major-league level. Where he once overwhelmed lesser hitters with velocity, now his fastball is a change-of-pace, finishing weapon after he has slowed hitters down with the other parts of his seven-pitch mix.</p><h3>Schultz up, Urquidy out</h3><p>Neither right-hander <b>Jose Urquidy</b> nor left-hander <b>Noah Schultz</b> had pitched in the last week, suggesting the former was without a steady role and the latter was getting ready for a call-up. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/white-sox-recall-noah-schultz-designated-jose-urquidy-for-assignment-will-venable-chris-getz-david-sandlin-division-race" target="_blank" >Urquidy was designated for assignment</a> to make room for Schultz, whose newly prescribed multi-inning relief role probably will be better understood after his first outing.</p><p>‘‘You’re looking at spots in the game where — we talked about it earlier today — you can envision a time through the order at least,’’ Venable said. ‘‘Kind of a multi-inning weapon.’’</p><p>Schultz had a 1.66 ERA in five starts in his latest minor-league stint and is excited about an improved changeup. Mostly, he seems happier to be part of a major-league playoff race than a Triple-A rotation.</p><p>‘‘It’s such an important time of the year,’’ Schultz said. ‘‘I’m doing, obviously, whatever I can to help contribute.’’</p><h3>Colson out of lineup vs. lefty</h3><p>At this point in his tenure, Venable playing to the platoon advantage is as sure as the sunrise. But left-handed-hitting infielder <b>Colson Montgomery</b> sitting against Guardians lefty <b>Foster Griffin</b> actually went against his season numbers. Montgomery has hit left-handers (.814 OPS) better than right-handers (.668).</p><p>Single-season platoon numbers can be pretty variable, though, and the Sox haven’t fully embraced the idea that Montgomery is wired differently.</p><p>‘‘I wouldn’t say we look at him as a reverse-split guy, even though I know that’s what his splits are this year,’’ Venable said. ‘‘But definitely more neutral, where we’re not as concerned about matchups with Colson.’’</p><p>The bigger issue is that Montgomery, who lined out and struck out after entering the game as a pinch hitter in the sixth inning, went into Tuesday hitting .109/.255/.283 with a 43.6% strikeout rate in September.</p>

announced Wednesday.</p><p>Called Vector, the angular, winding sculpture will be composed of glazed terra cotta panels — a contrast to the glassy and rounded headquarters and its now-muted exterior colors brought about by the building's current renovation.</p><p>"The quilt is interesting to me because it is sort of the repository of American culture, in a lot of ways," said Biggers, 56, a Los entries.title: 16-year-old boy shot twice in Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>A teenage boy was shot in Albany Park Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A 16-year-old was in the 4700 block of North Albany Avenue at 8:58 p.m. when he was shot in the left foot and abdomen, police said. </p><p>He transported himself to Swedish Hospital before being taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital, where he was listed in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. entries.title: Cubs’ latest bullpen blow-up stark reminder that without reliable relievers ‘we’re not going to survive’
entries.summary: <p>The night the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> were officially eliminated from the NL Central race, they received another stark reminder about their beleaguered bullpen:</p><p>“We’re not going to survive if we don’t have multiple guys we can count on,” manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>said Tuesday after a 6-3 loss to the Braves at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Counsell’s former team, the Brewers, clinched their fourth straight division title in Pittsburgh as his current team suffered through another bullpen meltdown, with right-handed relievers <b>Jacob Webb </b>and <b>Edward Cabrera </b>each serving up a two-run homer in the late innings against a playoff-caliber lineup.</p><p>Postseason survival is predicated on that sort of thing not happening, not with any sort of frequency, but that has been the story for the Cubs down the stretch.</p><p>With 10 games left on their regular-season schedule, it’s unclear which relievers they’ll be able to count on when the lights get even brighter in October.</p><p>It has been a particularly brutal stretch for Webb, who was so good as the Cubs’ go-to reliever earlier in the summer, at one point stringing together 24 consecutive scoreless appearances.</p><p>But the game-flipping homer he allowed in the seventh inning Tuesday, sending the Cubs from up a run to down a run, was the fourth long ball he has allowed in his last eight outings. His record dropped to 6-5 with the loss.</p><p>Cabrera was in his first relief appearance as a Cub, just back from a lengthy stint on the injured list dealing with blister issues as the Cubs try to find out in the waning days of the season if he can be a useful piece in a playoff bullpen.</p><p>Although his 2 1/3 innings were mostly good Tuesday, the homer he gave up in the ninth significantly dinged any chances at a comeback.</p><p>Of course, plenty contributes to such defeats, and the Cubs’ best-in-baseball bats couldn’t muster more than three runs and five singles on the evening, with their final dozen hitters going down in order.</p><p>But the glare of September baseball can’t help but illuminate their apparent Achilles’ heel — a relief corps that has been under the magnifying glass since Webb coughed up the first of two back-breaking walk-off homers on a road trip in late August.</p><p>In October, when the use of pitchers becomes a different beast with everything on the line, it will be impossible to survive performances like this one.</p><p>“We’ve got to put together 27 outs,” Counsell said. “We’ve got to get guys pitching well, and we’ve got to have guys we can count on, multiple guys we can count on.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox have moments to second-guess after crushing walk-off loss in Cleveland
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Something — or someone — produced a sound like a wall being punched inside the White Sox’ clubhouse after their game Tuesday.</p><p>The potential reasons for it — after the game flipped from what would have been a gutty comeback victory to clinch a vital series against the second-place Guardians to a crushing 7-6 loss on Brayan Rocchio’s second walk-off hit against closer Grant Taylor of the season — are innumerable.</p><p>‘‘It sucks,’’ said right-hander Davis Martin, who allowed two runs (one earned) in 5⅓ innings. ‘‘We did a lot of really good things tonight, but baseball doesn’t always reward you for doing everything right.’’</p><p>The final pitch alone, set up by a walk to light-hitting catcher Patrick Bailey that put the winning run aboard after Nathaniel Lowe had singled, spoke multitudes.</p><p>Taylor got ahead of Rocchio — the author of three previous walk-off hits this season — 0-2 with a pair of breaking balls. He followed with a 101 mph sinker well above the zone. Rocchio didn’t hit it especially hard, but the ball went high and far into the left-field corner, where it floated just out of Sam Antonacci’s diving attempt. MLB’s player tracking showed the converted infielder taking a short loop inward before righting his path and racing to the corner, a half-second too late.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Sam Antonacci postgame <a href="https://t.co/jpQ2vzstSe">pic.twitter.com/jpQ2vzstSe</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2100045272638185946?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>‘‘Pretty dog[-expletive], to be honest,’’ Antonacci said of his route. ‘‘Got to clean it up. It’s the big leagues. You can’t make those types of routes.’’</p><p>Manager Will Venable, however, was more understanding.</p><p>‘‘That’s not on Sammy; that’s a tough play,’’ Venable said. ‘‘A big play but not the reason that we lost that game.’’</p><p>Instead, Venable wondered about the pitch: a triple-digit fastball in a chase location but still a fastball to a hitter who had burned Taylor on the same pitch earlier this season.</p><p>‘‘You’ve seen Rocchio and even heard from him how he’s selling out to fastballs against Grant,’’ Venable said. ‘‘[He] had him 0-2 with a couple of breaking balls [and] tried to sneak one by him. Really good hitter, made contact and obviously saw the results.’’</p><p>‘‘I wouldn’t say [Rocchio] sold out to it,’’ catcher Kyle Teel said. ‘‘Two strikes on him, it’s the right pitch call. Grant’s throwing 101 mph. It is what it is. I liked the pitch call. I think Grant put it in a solid spot. If we spin him there and we throw three [breaking balls] in a row, he could clip that one, too.’’</p><p>The ninth inning wiped away the Sox’ comeback from an early 3-0 hole, as left-hander Chris Murphy was roughed up for a pair of home runs in the team’s league-leading 31st use of an opener. Martin might have been fine without the help, but a one-run loss had him kicking himself for an errant pickoff throw that skipped away from first baseman Munetaka Murakami in the fifth as Rocchio — who else? — raced home from third.</p><p>Even though the Sox ran up the pitch count against a Guardians starter for the second consecutive night and hung a crooked number against the bullpen in the sixth, the slim margin made Murakami’s 0-for-4, four-strikeout night impossible to hide.</p><p>‘‘It’s not like moving him in the lineup is going to magically fix his swing,’’ Venable said. ‘‘As you look at how we’re compiling our lineups and want to give yourself the best chance, he’s still a part of that.’’</p><p>Just as difficult as what the Sox lost is what lies ahead: a game for the American League Central lead Wednesday against Guardians All-Star Parker Messick, with Taylor, Sean Newcomb and Hagen Smith all having been used for multiple innings on successive nights.</p><p>Tuesday was the game the Sox were set up to win to guarantee leaving Cleveland in first place. But for a host of reasons, all aggravating in their own right, it slipped away.</p><p>‘‘You can’t just say, ‘Oh, it’s OK. We’ll brush it off,’ ’’ Martin said. ‘‘Feel it as long as you want to feel it and accept it. And then come back tomorrow hungry.’’</p>

entries.title: 'Broadview 6' say Boutros' 'significant failings' warrant special counsel probe of 'poisoned' case
entries.summary: <p>Four months after the spectacular collapse of the "Broadview Six" case, the onetime defendants argued Tuesday that "significant failings"<b> </b>by Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros demonstrate<b> </b>the need for an independent special counsel to figure out what went wrong with the tainted conspiracy case brought against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.</p><p>At "bare minimum,"<b> </b>they said, answers are needed about Boutros' recent admission that he possessed a transcript<b> </b>of grand jury proceedings during which one of his prosecutors engaged in apparent misconduct. It occurred while the feds were seeking an indictment against the six individuals who demonstrated last September against the Trump administration's aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>Boutros has said he doesn't remember reading the transcript when he got it last fall. And he told U.S. District Judge April Perry in May he'd only learned of the misconduct<b> </b>in April.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But defense attorneys hammered away at the revelation in a 61-page court document<b> </b>filed late Tuesday.</p><p>"The roots of this prosecution … were poisoned from the start," they wrote.</p><p>Their filing might finally bring an end to the monthslong<b> </b>back-and-forth between defense attorneys and prosecutors over what should be done about the “Broadview Six” case. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >May 21 collapse</a> of the case led to repeated calls for hearings over the conduct of Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg, the prosecutor at the center of the controversy. Questions also remain about the roles played by others in Boutros' office.</p><p>Now, with such questions fully briefed in the "Broadview Six" case, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >all eyes will turn to Perry</a>. </p><p>It's not clear how — or when — Perry will hand down a ruling, though. She could summon lawyers to her courtroom and hand it down from the bench. She might hold a hearing. Or, she might drop a written ruling on the court docket without warning.</p><p>Meanwhile, the new defense filing<b> </b>invites the judge<b> </b>to order prosecutors<b> </b>to turn over documents. Specifically,<b> </b>they suggest<b> </b>"any communications"<b> </b>between Boutros' office and Justice Department officials in Washington. The records could be turned over only to Perry, they wrote, for her review.</p><p>Along the way, defense attorneys raised several questions about the grand jury transcript possessed by Boutros. They pointed to his "tough stance on prosecuting individuals who purportedly assault law enforcement officers" and noted he'd "declared these cases to be of great significance."</p><p>The transcript in question recorded the events of Oct. 9, when grand jurors initially rejected the case against the "Broadview Six" in a rebuke known as a no-bill. Boutros has said he<b> </b>received<b> </b>a copy<b> </b>of that transcript<b> </b>by email<b> </b>Oct. 14.</p><p>"The government wants this court to believe that [Boutros] did not review the very crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV. But from that crowd, only six were charged. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" target="_blank" >The defendants</a> were then-congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Abughazaleh campaign worker Andre Martin.</p><p>The feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped charges</a> against Walsh and Sharp in March. Then, on the eve of trial in late May,<b> </b>defense attorneys convinced Perry to review unredacted transcripts of grand jury proceedings in the case. The feds had previously given her redacted versions.</p><p>Perry later said she was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >“incredibly shocked”</a><b> </b>to find three types of prosecutorial misconduct in the unredacted transcripts. Mecklenburg<b> </b>is accused of speaking with grand jurors outside the grand jury room and of excusing grand jurors who didn’t agree with the feds’ case. She’s also accused of a forbidden practice known as “vouching.”</p><p>It occurs when prosecutors put their personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges.</p><p>Perry concluded that her trust in federal prosecutors had “been broken.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Four weeks after Perry revealed what she’d found, defense attorneys for some of the former defendants asked Perry to take the extraordinary step of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >appointing<b> </b>a special counsel</a> to investigate Boutros<b> </b>and other Justice Department officials for criminal contempt.</p><p>Boutros has since acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" target="_blank" >“mistakes were made.”</a><b> </b>But he said he’s put reforms in place to prevent them from happening again. He noted his office is not accused of explicitly violating Perry’s order regarding the grand jury transcripts, but he admitted the “better course”<b> </b>would have been to give her unredacted copies of the grand jury transcripts in the first place.</p><p>Meanwhile, his office has worked to manage a credibility crisis that has not been limited to Perry’s courtroom. Multiple judges questioned their ability to trust federal prosecutors and agents this summer, and some threatened to hold hearings.</p><p>“The court’s message has been clearly heard and there is no need to do more,” Boutros told Perry in a 52-page court filing Aug. 4. “The office has not taken lightly this court’s statement about losing trust.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/52/c7/09aa531f4c60b1bb7f4682e351ff/usavrabbittbrief91526.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Chirping cicadas pique Chicago area's curiosity
entries.summary: <p>In a recent Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicadas-louder-mating-brood-decibels-coping-mechanisms-dog-days-summer-heat-trees" >article</a> headlined “Are cicadas louder this year?” one person wondered if more cicadas could be heard in Thatcher Woods, LaBagh Woods and Skokie Lagoons. The answer is yes, we do have more dog day cicadas singing this time of year compared to prior years, and they are indeed louder than usual.</p><p>As an insect ecologist who works for the Cook County Forest Preserves, I've been studying singing insects since 2015 with the assistance of colleagues, volunteers and Carl Strang, who wrote the book "Singing insects of the Chicago region." I lead sound walks in the Chicago area, helping people tune their ears to the variety of insect and wildlife song around us.</p><p>Cicadas started emerging later this summer compared to prior years, likely because of early season temperatures and rain fluctuations. Think of dinner service at a popular walk-up restaurant. Customers come in waves: the after-work crowd, friends wanting to catch up, after-show audiences. If an accident snarls traffic, and no one can get there before 7 p.m., the rest of the night is a lot busier. And louder! It’s the same with the dog day cicadas. Instead of starting to emerge in July and staggering their emergence throughout the summer, a bunch arrived fashionably late. The result? More at once, setting up a raucous September dog day cicada party.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://singinginsects.net/magicicada-soundmap-project/" target="_blank" >Magicicada Soundmap Project </a>volunteers have captured dog day cicada decibel levels ranging from 60 to 70 near their homes and forest preserves. In 2024, individual dog day cicadas were drowned out by airplanes and other human noise that hung around 40 to 50 decibels.</p><p>For anyone who wants in on the fun, the forest preserves and the <a class="Link" href="https://mwsae.org/" target="_blank" >Midwest Society for Acoustic Ecology</a> are hosting one last sound walk of the season Oct. 3. You can register <a class="Link" href="https://fpdcc.com/events/" target="_blank" >online</a> on the forest preserves' website. Volunteers interested in monitoring cicadas next year can send a note to <a class="Link" href="mailto:singinginsects@gmail.com" target="_blank" >singinginsects@gmail.com</a>.</p><p><i>Negin Almassi,</i> <i>Cook County Forest Preserves</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-410000" name="module-410000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Muslim pols hurdle political barriers</h3><p>In her latest <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/15/muslim-politics-democrat-trump-el-sayed-mamdani-piker-rummana-hussain" >column</a>, the Sun-Times' Rummana Hussain rightly pinpointed the recent wave of “young goateed” Muslim leaders like Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani who are subverting political norms and rattling the establishment by refusing to stay in neat little boxes.</p><p>There are moments in America when an election becomes a political crucible larger than the candidate. For Catholics, John F. Kennedy’s 1960 victory marked a turning point. His victory did not end anti-Catholic prejudice, but it shattered a barrier that had told generations of Catholics there were limits to how fully they could belong in public life. For Muslims, El-Sayed’s primary victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate race represents a similar breakthrough.</p><p>Post-9/11, a cloud of suspicion was systematically cast on Muslims. An entire generation witnessed our faith become synonymous with extremism and national security threats. Our loyalty was questioned, our mosques were <a class="Link" href="https://www.aclu.org/documents/surveillance-under-usapatriot-act" target="_blank" >surveilled</a> and our institutions were placed under intense scrutiny.</p><p>As Hussain noted, political opponents still reflexively use Trojan horse tropes or demand public disavowals from Muslim public figures. Having served in government on national security, I know that experience intimately. I can't count how many times peers on both the right and left implied that my loyalty to the United States came with an asterisk. Aspiring Muslim public servants often understood that entering government came with an implicit condition: We could enter political life, but only if we weren't too visibly Muslim or too critical of U.S. foreign policy.</p><p>Now, the political needle is moving. Rather than letting the “peanut gallery” trap him in identity politics, El-Sayed remains unshaken in his campaign <a class="Link" href="https://wdet.org/2026/08/11/abdul-el-sayed-metro-interview/" target="_blank" >messaging</a> regarding universal healthcare, money out of politics and affordability. Just like JFK, leaders like Mamdani and El-Sayed are no longer asking permission to belong.</p><p>My generation spent much of our adult lives trying to prove we belonged. Perhaps the next generation of Muslim children in Detroit, Queens or Chicago will look at leaders like Mamdani and El-Sayed and understand there is no contradiction between being deeply Muslim and deeply American.</p><p>If El-Sayed wins in November, he will make history. But the glass ceiling has already been shattered. A new generation of American Muslims has decided it will no longer allow prejudice to determine what is possible.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://archive.mpac.org/about/staff-board/haris-tarin/" target="_blank" ><i>Haris Tarin</i></a><i>, vice president, Muslim Public Affairs Council</i></p><h3>Art and AI </h3><p>I understand the concerns about artificial intelligence. Human art has value. Artists deserve to be paid for their work, and I understand why they’re protective of their craft.</p><p>What I don’t understand is how people can be mean about it. I’m seeing artists and small businesses shamed, called horrendous names and excluded from creative spaces because they used AI for a logo or promotional graphic.</p><p>There's a massive difference between a corporation replacing paid artists with AI to increase profits and a small business that needs a flyer but doesn't have the money to commission one. That doesn’t mean they don’t value artists. It means they’re broke.</p><p>Time matters too. Finding artists, waiting for responses, discussing the project, drafts and revisions takes time. Quality takes time. But we’re also running businesses. If we can create what we need in 20 minutes using the tools available to us, sometimes that's what we have to do.</p><p>Deciding who's “worthy” of creating based on access, money, time or tools starts looking a whole lot like elitism and gatekeeping.</p><p>If we want people to hire human artists instead of AI, we need realistic ways to do that. My business, Forever Feral Habitat, is creating a <a class="Link" href="tinyurl.com/HireHuman" target="_blank" >free public directory </a>connecting small businesses with human artists and creatives across different services, experience levels, prices and turnaround times.</p><p>If you’ve been telling people to stop using AI and hire human artists instead, help me build the alternative.</p><p>Bullying and exclusion aren't solutions.</p><p><i>Raina Kubinski, owner/artist, Forever Feral Habitat, Plainfield</i> <br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Neighbors are friendly, but mom doesn't want daughter visiting them
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My next-door neighbors are appropriately friendly, mow their lawn and generally mind their own business. The husband is a leader in a fundamentalist church whose pastor preaches that being gay is a sin and transgender people are mentally ill. My wife and I are lesbians, and our middle child is transgender. This is obvious to anyone who has met us.</p><p>Our third child is the same age as the neighbors' daughter, and they play outside sometimes. Her mom has started asking if my daughter can come over to their house. I'm looking for a kind way to let her know that playdates are not an option. I respect their family's right to have values different from mine, but I don't think it's emotionally safe for my kid to be over there. Similarly, my house is too queer-friendly for me to feel comfortable hosting a conservative neighbor's kid here. How do I give a blanket "no" to visits while remaining cordial neighbors? — <i>THE LESBIAN NEXT DOOR</i></p><p><b>DEAR LESBIAN NEXT DOOR:</b> I get the impression you and your neighbors are polite but not close, so there's your reason: Tell her you aren't comfortable letting your daughter spend time inside the home of someone you don't know well.</p><p>To improve this relationship, invite them over for dinner, perhaps a casual outdoor barbecue. If it turns out your two families are as incompatible as you suspect, your daughter will stop receiving playdate invitations.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My boyfriend, "Dirk," and I are in our late 50s. We both are divorced, and we each have a single child over the age of 18. Every time Dirk and I go out for a nice dinner date, he either orders a meal "to go" to bring home for his son or purposely eats only half his dinner and brings the rest home for him. I've told Dirk this is rude. It spoils the mood of having an intimate adult date. His son is old enough to figure out how to feed himself.</p><p>The problem is, Dirk won't stop doing this, and it's been going on for years. It took two years to finally get Dirk to stop bringing his son with us if we went on errands together. I feel suffocated and like I'm dating two rather than one in that household. Dirk chooses to blur boundaries and always pulls the "single dad, raising him on my own" card, an excuse I've never had to make. I believe it applies to minor children, not adults, and coddling to this extreme is ridiculous.</p><p>Am I being too harsh? My son is self-sufficient. He has a healthy social life and keeps healthy boundaries when it comes to my love life. I've talked myself hoarse being honest with Dirk about all of this, but it never changes, and these dynamics keep me from advancing my commitment to Dirk. He begs me to move in, but I think after one week, I'd be at my wits' end. Should I pull the plug altogether and move on? — <i>DATING TWO IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DATING:</b> I think that unless you'd like to become a family of three living under Dirk's roof, you need to do exactly that. Feeling as you do about Dirk's son, the relationship would be doomed from the moment you unpacked your bags.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Historic South Side building is the first to violate Chicago’s cooling ordinance this year
entries.summary: <p>City officials say the historic Yale Building at 6565 S. Yale Ave. became the first to violate Chicago’s cooling ordinance this year when its chiller broke down in late August.</p><p>“Following our inspection of 6565 S. Yale Ave., inspectors cited the property for an inoperable chiller and noncompliance with the City’s Cooling Ordinance,” wrote Nefsa'Hyatt Brown, director of public affairs for the city’s Department of Buildings, in a Sept. 3rd email. "[The Department of Buildings] has escalated our enforcement action to the Department of Law for Circuit Court.”</p><p>Records show the failed inspection occurred on Aug. 31. The first hearing in the case was held on Sept. 2. Landlords and building owners can be fined up to $1,000 per day, per violation.</p><p>After the tragic deaths of three elderly women at the James Sneider Apartments in Rogers Park in the summer of 2022, Chicago’s cooling ordinance was established to protect those who may be more vulnerable to heat. The ordinance requires certain buildings — including nursing homes, housing for older persons, high-rises over 80 feet, and residential buildings with 100 or more units — to “provide air conditioning in every unit, or maintain a designated air-conditioned common area available to residents when the heat index exceeds 80 degrees,” Brown wrote. "We have had 8 violations of the Chicago Cooling Ordinance referred to the City's Department of Law, including the most recent at 6565 S. Yale."</p><p>So far this year, 14 people have died from heat-related causes in Cook County, the most in any year since at least 2015. Eleven of the deaths have occurred in Chicago.</p><p>The Yale Building was constructed in Englewood, in the 1890s, and renovated into low-income senior housing in 2003. John Luce, the building’s owner, said that the 20-year-old, 100-ton chiller has been fixed and will be getting replaced this fall. In order to mitigate the situation, Luce said he provided more than 10 extra window air conditioning units to his residents. “I feel terrible about it,” he said.</p><p>On the afternoon of Sept. 9, a few residents said the building did get extremely hot during the previous week, but they said the cooling system had been fixed and there were no more issues. In the days following the failed inspection, Chicago experienced its warmest start to September ever with high temperatures topping 90°F on each of the month’s first four days, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>But Luce said he wasn’t aware of the cooling ordinance and the changed regulations. He said his property manager and a fellow building owner from a nearby area were also unaware of the changes. To his knowledge, Luce said they were only required to have air-conditioned common areas.</p><p>According to Luce, at the time of inspection, the building had two separate air-conditioned common areas, each with ice water and one air conditioner. Luce said the inspectors asked him to get one additional air conditioner in each common area, to which he complied. Luce said the inspectors measured the temperature of each apartment unit and around the building overall. At the end of the inspection, he said the city found the building to be noncompliant with the cooling ordinance.</p><p>“They need a segway to send information to us,” Luce said. “I just need to know if there is a change in the law.”</p><h3><b>Hundreds complain about ‘no air conditioning’ each year</b></h3><p>Soon after the Chicago City Council passed the cooling ordinance in June 2022, the city began logging complaints it receives from residents reporting that their buildings have no air conditioning.</p><p>According to Brown, the department received and resolved a total of 397 such complaints during June and July this year. “The Chicago Construction Code defines every building owner’s responsibility to keep mechanical systems, including cooling equipment, operable and maintained. Most of the air conditioning complaints [the department] receives fall under that broader responsibility,” Brown wrote in an email.</p><p>Brown noted that, previously this year, the department hadn’t issued a formal violation or filed a court action under the cooling ordinance. “That is not because problems do not occur,” Brown wrote. “It is because they are resolved quickly through repair and voluntary compliance, often with the [department of buildings] on site, before they reach an escalated level of enforcement.”</p><p>A WBEZ analysis of city data shows hundreds of Chicagoans have filed no air conditioning complaints through the city’s 311 nonemergency hotline each year for the past several years. In all, more than 1,900 such complaints have been filed since the passage of the cooling ordinance in June 2022.</p><p>Nearly 1,000 buildings have logged at least one complaint during that span. The Yale Building ranks fourth overall with 23 complaints. City data show three complaints for the building have been filed this year: one on July 20; one on Aug. 31, the day the building was inspected and found noncompliant with the cooling ordinance; and one on Sep. 2.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-320000" name="html-embed-module-320000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/30207278"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30207278/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Ald. Maria Hadden (49th), who introduced the cooling ordinance, pointed out that climate change is the reason why these buildings are vulnerable to heat. She said that many buildings were built almost a 100 years ago, and the heat that Chicago experienced at the time wasn’t as intense or frequent.</p><p>“There’s a reason why so many of our residential buildings, school buildings, park districts, they’ve all been retrofitted with air conditioning or cooling systems,” Hadden said. “In many respects, we don’t seem prepared for it. Individuals aren’t prepared. Systems aren’t prepared.”</p><p>The Department of Buildings advises residents to file a report by calling 311, if they believe their building is not meeting cooling requirements. Leaving detailed 311 reports with contact information, as well as having multiple neighbors in the same building file separate reports, can help establish the scope of the problem. The department also advises property owners to prepare early and inspect their cooling systems.</p>

entries.title: Chaka Khan's very good 2026 includes a new album with Sia
entries.summary: <p>To see Chaka Khan perform is to be both enthralled by her icon status and charmed by her approachability.</p><p>In June, she took the stage at First Avenue in Minneapolis as part of “Prince Celebration: 2026,” a week-long tribute to her late friend and collaborator. Sporting her signature, glowing smile and voluminous tresses, she would hit an otherworldly note, then turn around and crack a joke, tell a story or ask for a moment to blow her nose.</p><p>“I’m actually a real person,” said the 73-year-old Chicago native as she giddily previewed tracks from her new album, “Chakzilla,” co-written with Sia and due out Friday.</p><p>“What do you think?’ she asked the audience, as a DJ played “Boogie’s in My Soul,” her single with Snoop Dogg, and “Curious Subject,” featuring lyrics about her enduring appeal.</p><p><i>Don't you wanna get to know me? entries.title: More people than ever are trying to get into college classes in Illinois prisons. It hasn't gotten easier.
entries.summary: <p>Access to college classes in Illinois prisons is falling further behind demand, even as the state makes progress getting people into GED and literacy programs. That’s according to <a class="Link" href="https://idoc.illinois.gov/reportsandstatistics/annual-report-for-higher-education.html" target="_blank" ><u>data published</u></a> by the Illinois Department of Corrections at the beginning of September.</p><p>The number of people on educational waitlists significantly exceeds the number taking classes. Since last year, the number of people on the waitlist for college classes has increased by 80%.</p><p>Around 2,600 out of the approximately 30,000 people incarcerated in Illinois are enrolled in higher education, while another 3,700 are on a waitlist, according to IDOC.</p><p>"That's a pretty powerful indication that the challenge isn't a lack of interest in education — it's our capacity to meet that interest," said Ashton Klekamp, policy and research director at the Education Justice Project at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, which offers college classes at Danville Correctional Center.</p><p>Research shows that <a class="Link" href="https://www.mackinac.org/pressroom/2023/research-finds-prison-education-programs-reduce-recidivism" target="_blank" ><u>participating in education</u></a> while incarcerated helps people find employment after release and reduces the likelihood they'll return to prison. In Illinois, some people who complete educational programs can also <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampus.org/2026/01/05/no-good-time-for-you-the-recordkeeping-problem-keeping-people-locked-up-longer/" target="_blank" ><u>earn credit</u></a> toward an earlier release.</p><p>The state’s enrollment figures include both college classes and career and technical education, as well as around 750 people on supervised release — Illinois' version of parole. It’s unclear if those on supervised release are studying at outside colleges, or if they are enrolled in programs behind bars.</p><p>This is the second year Illinois has published this data. In 2023, lawmakers passed legislation requiring the Illinois Department of Corrections to publish detailed data each yearabout enrollment, waitlists and spending on educational programs. It’s one of the few states that require corrections departments to publicly report such data.</p><h3><b>Who’s studying behind bars in Illinois</b></h3><p>White people are significantly overrepresented in higher education relative to the overall prison population, while Black and Hispanic people are underrepresented. White people make up over a third of the prison population but nearly half of those studying. Black people, by contrast, make up more than half of the prison population but only 43% of higher education participants. Hispanic people make up 13% of the prison population but only 10% of participants.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe title="Illinois Department of Corrections Population Data" aria-label="Grouped column chart" id="datawrapper-chart-VcRrw" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VcRrw/2/" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="width: 0; min-width: 100% !important; border: none;" height="533" data-external="1"></iframe><script type="text/javascript">(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();</script> </div> </div></div><p>About 160 women are enrolled in prison higher education programs here, and their enrollment is roughly the same as their share of Illinois’ prison population. However, the number of women participating in education declined by about a quarter since last year.</p><p>The average person enrolled in higher education is 39 years old with about 4.4 years left on their sentence — consistent with the state's practice of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/criminal-justice/2025/06/19/mans-18-year-journey-to-get-his-ged-while-locked-up-illinois-prisons" target="_blank" ><u>prioritizing people closest to release</u></a> for educational programming.</p><p>"For a long time … we didn't have a sense of where that access existed and who didn't have access," Klekamp said. "The demographic data is something that is really important…People are telling us very clearly that they want an education. The question for Illinois is whether we're willing to build the capacity to meet that demand."</p><h3><b>Geography matters</b></h3><p>Whether someone has access to higher education depends largely on geography.</p><p>“One of the things that jumps out immediately is how uneven access is across facilities,” Klecamp said. “It tells us that the experience of trying to access education can depend considerably on where someone is incarcerated."</p><p>The average wait for a spot has dropped since last year, from about 1.3 years to roughly 324 days, a shift possibly driven by a surge of new applicants on lists. IDOC spokesperson Naomi Puzzello attributed the growth in applicants to more people successfully completing the academic placement test required for programs and therefore being eligible for higher education.</p><p>Danville Correctional Center now has the longest average wait in the system, at nearly 5.5 years. Logan, Illinois’ largest women’s prison which offers a bachelor's degree through Northwestern University, follows closely at just under 4.9 years.</p><p>Several people in prison have been waiting years to get enrolled in prison higher education programs.</p><p>At Big Muddy River prison, one person has been on the waitlist since October 2006 — the longest wait Open Campus found in the data, at nearly 19 years. Several other facilities — including Dixon, Pinckneyville, Taylorville, and Western Illinois — have people who were put on waitlists between 2016 and 2019.</p><p>Many of the people with the longest waits remain at the bottom of the lists under the system's release-based approach. The individual who has waited longest of all, at Big Muddy River, has no listed sentence length in the data — which typically indicates a life sentence or similarly indefinite term.</p><p>Some facilities have especially large waitlists because they host several college programs at once. Sheridan Correctional Center is the clearest example, where 78% of the population is either studying or waiting for a spot. Its waitlist has grown since the facility absorbed Northwestern's bachelor's program and other college offerings after <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampus.org/2024/08/20/what-will-the-stateville-shutdown-mean-for-higher-education-programs-behind-bars/" target="_blank" ><u>Stateville’s 2024 closure</u></a>.</p><p>Other facilities have no waitlists because they offer little to no higher education programming in the first place. Menard, in southern Illinois, has just 8 people enrolled and 8 on the waitlist; its only offerings are <a class="Link" href="https://idoc.illinois.gov/facilities/allfacilities/facility.menard-correctional-center.html" target="_blank" ><u>two career and technical tracks</u></a>, in building and construction maintenance and small engine repair. Pontiac, in central Illinois, has <a class="Link" href="https://idoc.illinois.gov/facilities/allfacilities/facility.pontiac-correctional-center.html" target="_blank" ><u>no higher education programming at all</u></a> and almost no one on its waitlist.</p><p>Puzzello said IDOC is "consistently working to expand academic opportunities" and remains open to partnering with higher education providers interested in offering programs at facilities like these.</p><h3><b>Progress on GED and literacy programs and more funding for state colleges</b></h3><p>The state appears to be making progress getting people into GED and literacy programs. The waitlist for these programs shrank slightly this year compared to 2025, even as participation held roughly steady. Puzzello said the decline is due to increased staffing, improved movement between facilities, and a higher GED pass rate.</p><p>Illinois lawmakers have begun <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=111&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=155787&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>directing state money</u></a> toward public colleges and universities offering higher education in prison. The state's 2027 budget included $250,000 for the Illinois Board of Higher Education to help fund bachelor's degree programs in prisons, and another $250,000 for the Illinois Community College Board to help fund associate degree programs.</p><p>Currently, the majority of bachelor's degree programs in Illinois prisons come through private universities — Northwestern, Lewis, Adler and Augustana all offer bachelor's degrees. North Park Theological Seminary offers a master’s degree in restorative justice ministries.</p><p>The only four-year public institutions offering credit-bearing academic courses are University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, which offers college credit but not a full degree, and Eastern Illinois University. Both operate at Danville Correctional Center. Community college programming, meanwhile, is <a class="Link" href="https://www.iccb.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Annual_IDOC_Enroll_Comp_2025.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>overwhelmingly concentrated in career and technical education</u></a> rather than academic coursework and offered by just three colleges.</p><p>Puzzello wrote that the department is "requesting that colleges reinstate academic courses using the appropriated funds." She added that IDOC expects higher education staffing to increase as community colleges reinstate academic courses, though she did not specify which courses or facilities that refers to.</p><p><i>This story was produced in partnership with </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampus.org/college-inside/" target="_blank" ><i><u>Open Campus</u></i></a><i>, a nonprofit newsroom covering higher education. It's published in partnership with WBEZ's </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/prisoncast-illinois" target="_blank" >Prisoncast!</a><i>, an audio journalism project made with and for incarcerated people and their loved ones.</i></p>

entries.title: 10 jazz sets to see this month at Chicago’s free festivals, from up-and-comers to John Coltrane tributes
entries.summary: <p>Chicago has had an especially big year for jazz, beginning when the city hosted the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/04/15/unesco-international-jazz-day-chicago-music-kurt-elling-herbie-hancock-best-venues" target="_blank" ><u>UNESCO International Jazz Day</u></a> in April. But local fans of the genre know that September is the city’s true jazz month, when three free festivals unfold across town.</p><p>While Downtown’s city-run Chicago Jazz Festival has come and gone for the year, there is still plenty of world-class jazz performances on deck for this month.</p><p>This weekend, the 27th annual <a class="Link" href="https://englewoodjazzfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Englewood Jazz Festival</u></a>, founded by the esteemed saxophonist Ernest Dawkins, will uplift up-and-coming musicians, including members of the longstanding training ensemble, the Young Masters. The event also will celebrate all-time greats like John Coltrane and Miles Davis, who were both born 100 years ago.</p><p>Then, later in September, the <a class="Link" href="https://hydeparkjazzfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Hyde Park Jazz Festival</u></a> will ring in its 20th year. With so much free music to be heard, we’ve rounded up 10 sets you won’t want to miss at these South Side festivals.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://englewoodjazzfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Englewood Jazz Festival </u></b></a></h3><p><b>When: </b>Sept. 17-19, with music starting at 5:30 p.m. on Thursday and Friday and noon on Saturday<br><b>Where:</b> Hamilton Park, 513 W. 72nd St.</p><p>The <b>Julius Tucker Trio</b> will kick off the festival inside the park’s cultural center. The pianist and composer has become a staple of Chicago’s local jazz scene.
